extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in sociology, criminology, media studies, and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and unpack the core images, themes and ideological paradigms (the 'traditionalist' cluster and its rivals) that structure public opinion and media representations of crime in English society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant interpretations / institutional sources shaping public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Dominant interpretations’ are a powerful, indeed determining source in the analysis of how public opinion is formed; the so‑called 'conversation' from which public opinion arises is structured by its institutional sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that public opinion is not purely spontaneous but is heavily shaped by institutional actors and dominant frames; emphasizes attention to how institutions structure what appears to be 'public' debate and which viewpoints gain circulation and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of media processing of crime topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime topics are processed through stages: primary-news construction; passage into the domain of exploration and explanation ('second-order' news or feature treatment); and passage into the domain of judgement — the arena of the editorial statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-stage model when analysing media coverage: identify how a story is initially constructed, how it is reworked into interpretive/feature pieces, and how it is settled into editorial judgement; at each stage different structures of interpretation and ideological work operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological inflection across media outlets and points in process
rubrics_metrics.description: Different papers (and different points in the media process) display differences in ideological inflection and different structures of interpretation around the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare outlets and stages to see how ideological coloring shifts (e.g., tabloid splash vs feature length analysis vs editorial); attend to both content differences and the interpretive frameworks each outlet privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'circle' of public opinion — apparent spontaneity vs structured formation
rubrics_metrics.description: What appears as an apparently 'spontaneous' swell of opinion is in fact shaped: the 'circle' of public opinion (interpretations passing down and up) is not a miraculous spontaneous process but is structured by institutional forces and circulating ideological premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims of purely grassroots spontaneity; trace flows of interpretation upwards and downwards and identify institutional mediation (e.g., press, letters, local reports) that create the appearance of spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological paradigms underpinning public opinions about crime
rubrics_metrics.description: A far more limited set of ideological paradigms (themes, premises, assumptions, 'question–answer' matrices) generate the variety of public opinions about crime, giving coherence to diverse views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing public discourse, map the deeper paradigms (not just surface rhetoric) that recur across classes, media forms and expressive genres; these paradigms explain why diverse actors converge on similar interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditionalist versus liberal perspectives on crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Public discourse is organised around competing perspectives — notably a 'traditionalist' view (often dominant) and a 'liberal' perspective; the chapter focuses on how the traditionalist consensus is formed and reproduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish empirical expressions of opinion from the underlying perspective (traditionalist vs liberal); analyse mechanisms (media, institutions, class relations) by which one perspective generalises or fails to generalise across society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster: family, discipline and morality as organising themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and public reactions often form clusters organised around questions of the family, discipline and morality in relation to crime — a recurrent thematic cluster in the 'traditionalist' position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or interpreting public responses, look for this cluster of themes as a coherent package that mobilises moral language (family breakdown, lack of discipline, moral failing) in explanations of crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectability as a core image
rubrics_metrics.description: Respectability is a complex social idea touching self-respect, thrift, self-discipline, living the 'decent' life, self-help and conformity to established social standards; it functions as a key traditionalist value and 'cement' of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'respectability' as an analytic category to explain moral condemnation of deviants and the framing of crime as loss of respectability; consider class-specific articulations (middle-class emphasis on appearances, working-class link to regular work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work / the 'calculus of work' as an ideological image
rubrics_metrics.description: Work is represented as the guarantee of respectability: the 'calculus of work' implies beliefs like 'a fair day's wage for a fair day's work' and that valued goods are rewards for diligent labour; crime is contrasted with legitimate work and seen as illicitly gaining what others earn by toil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret anti-crime sentiments that invoke work—‘scrounger’, ‘layabout’—as moral evaluations grounded in the work calculus; note that this frame can carry both conservative and progressive implications (critique of unearned wealth vs condemnation of welfare recipients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social discipline (self-discipline) as central image
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for social discipline — especially internalised self-discipline (guilt, conscience, obedience, super-ego) — is a central image: discipline links to hierarchy, authority and the maintenance of order; indiscipline is read as seed-bed of anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse narratives about crime that invoke discipline/self-control; note class-variant meanings (middle-class emphasis on self-making, working-class emphasis on thrift and collective resilience) and the moral panic around youth as perceived indiscipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family as primary locus of socialisation and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The family is depicted as the sphere where moral-social compulsions and inner controls are generated (repression/regulation of sexuality, primary socialisation, patriarchal authority); it is seen as the 'factory' producing obedience and self‑discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat family-discourse as central to traditionalist explanations of crime (blame for breakdown of discipline, youth deviance); attend to how family ideology interlocks with images of sexuality, gender roles and moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image of the city and local ties
rubrics_metrics.description: The city embodies industrial civilisation and both wealth and its threats (disease, crime, unrest); working‑class experience of the city is parochial and local, and crime's registration in local space destabilises patterns of social ordering and produces strong anxieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing public reactions, consider scale: national/metropolitan images of the city differ from local neighbourhood attachments; crime that threatens local patterns of life provokes potent responses tied to place‑based identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal image of England (core national virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal idea of England: a core set of national virtues ('decent', 'tolerant', 'practical', 'pull together in crisis') that underpins claims to universality and provides emotional purchase across classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this national‑virtue frame to explain how diverse groups accept traditionalist claims as 'common sense' — appeals to 'Englishness' and shared character supply rhetorical authority during moral panics.

rubrics_metrics.name: External/imperial image of England (superiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: An external, imperial image of England that asserts English superiority and a 'civilising burden' rooted in imperial history; this quietly informs attitudes toward 'others' (immigrants, former colonised peoples) and racialised constructions of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how imperial nostalgia and assumptions of superiority shape racialised and xenophobic dimensions of crime discourse; watch for coded language and the unspoken hierarchy that situates 'English' as normative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional-world inflections on crime discourse (police, courts, social work, criminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different professional actors speak different idioms about street crime: the police use language of containment; the courts use judicial reasoning; social work uses social-care language; criminology/local councils have their own inflections — all strongly shaping opinions expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing media and public discourse, identify the professional voice(s) being invoked or quoted; these frames bring their own premises and interpretive repertoires which then circulate into public debate.
